title: Less friction
hook: small bits of effort shape behavior more than willpower

segments.voice: Yesterday, habits live in places, and your line was the place holds it. Did you go back to the spot you picked? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-seven.

A cafeteria line, lunchtime. Trays sliding along a rail. Researchers quietly move one dish a little farther back, just beyond easy reach. Nobody hides it. Nobody makes a rule. Anyone who wants it only has to lean in. And people take less of it. Not because they made a resolution, or summoned some inner strength. Because of a lean. Habit researchers draw a strange lesson from studies like this one: the tiniest bit of extra effort, a step, a reach, a second click, can move behavior more than all the willpower anyone brought to lunch.
screen: `A DISH, A LITTLE FARTHER BACK.` → `NOBODY MAKES A RULE.` → `PEOPLE TAKE LESS.`

segments.voice: First, the reach. In cafeteria studies, researchers led by Paul Rozin found that making a food slightly harder to get to, a little farther away, reduced how much of it people took. A small change in distance, a real change in behavior. Second, friction beats will, or so habit researchers argue. Psychologists who study habit, Wendy Wood among them, call these small costs friction. Willpower is what people tend to reach for first, and it can be unreliable. Friction works quietly, without asking anyone to try harder. The lean, the extra step, the drawer that has to be opened. Third, add friction to what you'd rather do less. The phone charging in another room. The snacks on a high shelf. Each one isn't a ban, just a small hill to climb, and small hills turn out to matter. Fourth, take friction away from what you want to do more. The running shoes by the door. The cushion already on the floor. The book on the pillow instead of the shelf. William James, in his chapter on habit, wrote: "The great thing, then, in all education, is to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy." Friction is one of the plainest ways to do that. Instead of fighting yourself every morning, you rearrange the room so the easy thing and the good thing are the same thing. A practice that needs a heroic effort to begin may not survive a busy week. A practice that's one step away has a fighting chance.
screen: `A LITTLE FARTHER AWAY.` · `FRICTION BEATS WILL.` · `A SMALL HILL FOR WHAT YOU WANT LESS.` · then, large: `ALLY INSTEAD OF ENEMY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one step easier. Sit and settle on the breath. Then think through tomorrow's practice, step by step, the way it actually happens. Where do you have to go? What do you have to find, open, unlock, set up? Look for the one step that most often stops you. Then picture removing it: the cushion left out, the app moved to the first screen, the alarm set the night before. Choose one. Just one. Then let the planning go and rest on the breath. The bell holds the time.
Less friction. Small bits of effort shape what people do more than willpower, so make the good thing one step easier. Today's word.

Your line: less friction. Today, before bed, do the one thing you chose: put the cushion out, set the book down, clear the step. Let tomorrow morning find the path already open. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: People building a habit sometimes arrange their surroundings so the practice takes as few steps as possible, leaving out what they need the night before, and put small obstacles in the way of habits they want to do less.

fork.setup: you keep meaning to meditate in the morning, but the cushion is in the closet behind the vacuum. what do you do?
options: leave the cushion out on the floor tonight.
decide meditation just isn't for you.
fork.reveal: take one step of friction away. habit researchers argue small effort changes move behavior more than willpower does.

trapdoor: what you thought: good habits come down to willpower.
what it means: small bits of effort, friction, quietly shape what people do, so you can rearrange them.
what a scholar hears: in the cafeteria studies, a slight change in reach changed intake; James had already framed habit as making the nervous system an ally.

notes: Confirm Rozin et al.: making foods slightly less accessible (a small change in distance, or switching tongs for spoons) reduced intake in a cafeteria setting. The hook scene is a simplified version of this.
Confirm James's wording in ch. IV exactly.
Attribution of the 'friction' framing to Wendy Wood is via her popular book; confirm or cut her name.
The script says only that willpower 'can be unreliable', avoiding the contested ego-depletion claim that it is a tiring resource.

Editor pass: 'studies keep finding' that friction beats willpower reframed as an argument habit researchers make (the cafeteria study measured reach, not willpower), in the hook, teach and fork reveal.
